A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DCT research. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original conditional-independence simulations, causal-discovery experiments, robustness evaluations, and a Big Five Personality data analysis in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulation and causal-discovery results, revised error-rate comparisons, and the retained robustness and Big Five analyses in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

M1.justification: DCT retains binarization, the same covariance bridge equations, nodewise regression, and asymptotic independence tests. Separating the monotone transformation from thresholding and correcting formulas against existing appendix derivations clarify the procedure rather than introduce a new algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Gaussian simulations, continuous/discrete/mixed observations, causal-discovery tasks, non-Gaussian and nonlinear scenarios, denser graphs, altered means/variances, and Big Five variables. New introductory application examples are not additional evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: Fisher-Z and chi-square remain the evaluated baselines. Causal-discovery comparisons retain Fisher-Z on undiscretized data as a reference. Figure 2's expanded legend labels an already plotted discretization-level comparator; additional citations do not introduce evaluated methods.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the power-comparison protocol: v3 empirically calibrates all tests to the desired Type I error level before reporting Type II errors, replacing v1's common nominal-threshold comparison. This substantially changes the interpretation of the main power benchmark; sample-size and conditioning-set grids remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The sample-size and conditioning-set sensitivity analysis now uses calibrated Type II errors, revising its evidence about power sensitivity. The non-Gaussian/nonlinear, graph-density, mean/variance, and real-data analyses are retained from v1 Appendix B in v3 Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 1,500 repetitions for the independence-test simulations and 10 graph instances with different seeds for causal discovery, reporting means and standard deviations. No new uncertainty-reporting practice, confidence interval, or comparative significance analysis is introduced.

E6.justification: Figure 2 substantially revises the error-rate results. At n=2000, discrete binary Fisher-Z and chi-square have calibrated Type II errors around 0.4 in v3, versus near-zero uncalibrated errors in v1. Some Type I curves also change. The stated satisfactory-power sample size changes from 2000 to 1000; this is not a same-protocol performance gain. Other causal-discovery and appendix results are retained.

T1.justification: v3 adds Theorem 2.1 and its Appendix A.1 proof asserting that discretizing the conditioning variable destroys conditional independence. It also corrects block-inverse identities in the nodewise-regression derivation and revises Taylor-expansion and vectorization formulas. The original asymptotic test theorems remain.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: recovering latent conditional independence despite discretization, covering continuous, discrete, and mixed observations, with theoretical and empirical support. Explicit nonparanormal terminology and rewritten contribution bullets principally reframe this existing scope.

C2.justification: v1 already acknowledged information loss from binarization and examined Gaussian-assumption violations. v3 Section 3.4 adds a concrete explanation of failure under nonlinear dependence using a quadratic example. Section 3.1 also explicitly links tailored bridge functions to potential improvements in sample efficiency.

D1.justification: New Appendices B and E identify Causal-learn as an implementation basis and disclose Xeon E5-2680 v4 hardware, 55 processors, and a reported four-hour runtime. These are additional reproducibility disclosures, not evidence of changed computational settings.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for nonparanormal modeling, nodewise regression, statistical foundations, and motivating applications. The substantive comparison with Fan et al. (2017), including the claimed gap concerning a conditional-independence test, remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten. Problem setting becomes a separate section, related work moves to Appendix D, and the document gains an assumptions discussion, appendix contents, resource section, and limitations section. These substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is rearranged, Figure 2 is redrawn with revised axes and legend, and Figures 3–4 regroup the existing causal-discovery panels by skeleton versus DAG, moving DAG results to Appendix B. Appendix figures are rescaled and relocated.

improvement.justification: Calibration improves the fairness of power comparisons, while algebraic corrections, clearer exposition, and resource disclosures provide further benefits. However, new Theorem 2.1 is false under its stated assumptions: mutually independent Gaussian variables satisfy its premises but remain independent after discretizing the conditioning variable. Its proof does not ensure the covariance factor is nonzero. These substantive benefits and the added theoretical defect leave the net quality change uncertain.
